analysis.investment_thesis: Cemindia (formerly ITD Cementation) shows genuinely impressive returns — ROCE of 27.6% and ROE of 21.8% are rare in the construction sector — but the business is project-based, government-dependent, and carries D/E of 0.48, all of which conflict with my need for predictable, low-debt compounders. A recent parent change to Renew Exim DMCC raises governance questions I cannot yet answer.
key_strengths: ROCE of 27.6% and ROE of 21.8% are exceptional for a construction company and suggest real capital efficiency and pricing power in specialised niches (maritime, tunnelling, foundations)
Revenue has accelerated sharply from INR 2,728 Cr (FY21) to INR 9,097 Cr (FY25), and order book growth implies near-term revenue visibility
Promoter holding of 67.46% is healthy and signals alignment
key_risks: Operating margin of 7.74% is thin and highly susceptible to input cost inflation, project delays, or cost overruns — one or two bad projects can wipe out a year's profit
FCF of only INR 30 Cr in FY25 against net profit of INR 373 Cr is a stark divergence; working capital intensity in construction means reported profits routinely differ from cash reality
Business model is entirely dependent on government and quasi-government capex cycles, which are politically unpredictable
red_flags: D/E of 0.48 exceeds my conservative limit of 0.3, and borrowings have risen from INR 458 Cr (FY21) to INR 982 Cr (FY25) in step with revenue — leverage is growing, not shrinking
Parent changed from Thai conglomerate ITD to Renew Exim DMCC in 2025 — a new, lesser-known promoter at the top of a fast-growing business warrants caution on governance integrity
Earnings quality is questionable: cash conversion ratio (FCF/Net Profit) collapsed to 8% in FY25, suggesting aggressive revenue/profit recognition on long-duration projects
analysis.detailed_analysis: The return ratios here are genuinely attractive and suggest a moat in specialised civil engineering (ports, tunnels, underground metro works) where few competitors exist. Revenue has more than tripled in four years, and EBITDA has followed. However, I do not invest in businesses I cannot underwrite for a decade, and construction cash flows are inherently lumpy and dependent on government priorities — not the steady, predictable compounding I seek for a core holding.
